say.text: A 70 kg adult with 40% burns is on a crystalloid drip set at 700 mL/h, the formula's starting rate.
Three hours in, urine is 15 mL/h. What do you do with the rate?

choices.label: Keep 700 mL/h, as the formula set it
Raise the rate by about a fifth and recheck in an hour
Cut the rate by about a fifth to spare the kidneys
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Low urine means the tissues are under-filled, so the rate goes up.
The formula gave a starting point. The urine tells you each hour whether to keep going.

choices.label: Sure of this? Skip the why

say.text: That choice is not right. Once the sum is worked, holding the rate looks settled, but a formula is only an estimate.
Look at this patient's urine number before you decide.

sure_note.text: You were sure of this one. A formula gives a starting rate; it does not replace reading the patient. Check the urine each hour.

say.text: That choice is not right. Cutting fluid when output falls looks careful, but it reads the number the wrong way.
Ask what a low urine reading says about the fluid already given.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction. Urine output is a gauge of perfusion, so work out what low output means.

say.text: Read the urine as a gauge of perfusion, not of how much the patient is losing. What does a low reading say the tissues are short of?
Low urine means under-perfusion, so the rate goes up by about a fifth. Recheck the urine each hour and move the rate with it.
The formula is a starting estimate, not a prescription to hold.
The Parkland formula gives a number from weight and burn size.
Why is that result only a starting estimate?

choices.label: The formula is exact, so only a wrong sum needs correcting
It covers 8 hours only; the rest follows a fixed protocol rate
Needs vary with depth, delay and inhalation, so urine guides it
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The sum is set by weight and burn size, but real need moves with depth, delay and the airway.
Hourly urine output tracks that movement, so it is what you titrate to.
That choice is not right. The sum leaves out depth, delay and inhalation injury, so it cannot be exact.
Ask what the sum does not know about the patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure the formula was exact. It is built from two inputs only, so it cannot know the rest.

say.text: That choice is not right. Nothing in the formula fixes a protocol rate for the later hours.
Ask what actually sets the rate in each hour.

sure_note.text: You were sure a fixed rate follows. Check what drives the rate hour by hour across the whole 24 hours.

say.text: What else about the patient, apart from the size of the burn, changes how much fluid they need?
Fluid need varies with burn depth, delay before resuscitation and inhalation injury. The sum is a start.
Hourly urine output guides the rate.
A 20 kg child has a 25% scald.
What hourly urine output do you aim for?

choices.label: 30 to 50 mL/h, the usual adult range
10 mL/h, half a mL per kilogram per hour
20 mL/h, about 1 mL per kilogram per hour
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. In a child the target is per kilogram, and it is higher than the adult figure.
Twenty kilograms at about 1 mL/kg/h gives about 20 mL/h.
That choice is not right. Halving the adult figure looks like a standard rule, but it is the adult per-kilogram number reused.
Check which number belongs to a child.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the child figure. The per-kilogram number you used is the adult one.

say.text: That choice is not right. The adult range is the number most people remember, but it is set for an adult body.
A child's target comes from the child's kilograms.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age qualifier. The adult range does not transfer to a child.

say.text: Two things change for a child: body weight and the kidneys. Which of these should set the number?
A child's target is about 1 mL/kg/h. At 20 kg that is about 20 mL/h.
The adult 0.5 mL/kg/h and the 30 to 50 mL/h range do not transfer to a child.
A 70 kg adult has an electrical burn and dark, pigmented urine. Rhabdomyolysis, muscle breakdown, is suspected.
What hourly urine output do you aim for?

choices.label: 20 mL/h, the figure used for a child
75 to 100 mL/h, set high to clear pigment
30 to 50 mL/h, the routine adult target
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The aim is a higher urine flow to clear myoglobin, which overrides the routine adult figure.
That choice is not right. The routine target is the easy default, but it does not fit this injury.
Ask what the kidneys have to clear after muscle breakdown.

sure_note.text: You were sure the routine figure covered it. Check what rhabdomyolysis asks of the kidneys.

say.text: That choice is not right. The child figure was the last rule you used, but this patient is a 70 kg adult.
Ask what the infusion is for here.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the child figure. Check who the patient is and why the fluid is running.

say.text: Ask what the target is for here: matching a routine, or clearing pigment from the kidneys?
Electrical injury with myoglobinuria needs about 1 to 1.5 mL/kg/h, around 75 to 100 mL/h in an adult, to flush out pigment.
Alkalinising the urine is not routinely needed if the output is adequate.
A junior charted a 3-year-old's total body surface area (TBSA) as 30% by the adult rule of nines.
What is wrong with that figure?

choices.label: The adult chart is the standard, so 30% stands at any age
Children are small adults, so the same proportions hold
A child's head and legs carry different shares of the total
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A child's head and legs carry different shares, so adult sums mis-state a child's burn.
Re-estimate the burn before you calculate any fluid.
That choice is not right. The adult chart is the one learned first, but its values are fixed for an adult body.
Ask whether a child's proportions match.

sure_note.text: You were sure the adult chart applies. Check the patient's age before the chart.

say.text: That choice is not right. A child looks like a small adult, but proportions change with age.
Ask which body parts change most between a child and an adult.

sure_note.text: You were sure a child is a small adult. Body proportions are not a scaled copy.

say.text: Which parts of the body are proportionally larger or smaller in a 3-year-old than in an adult?
A child's head is larger, about 18%, and each leg smaller, about 14%, than the adult figures.
The adult chart overstates the legs and understates the head. Re-estimate with a Lund and Browder chart before you set the fluid.
A 50 kg adult has a 40% burn and reaches you two hours after the burn. The ambulance has run 1,000 mL of Ringer lactate.
What rate do you set for the rest of the first 8 hours?

choices.label: 500 mL/h, the 3,000 mL still owed over six hours
375 mL/h, the 3,000 mL still owed over eight hours
670 mL/h, the full 4,000 mL over six hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Half the 24-hour total is due in the first 8 hours from the burn, and fluid already given counts toward it.
Run only what remains, over the time that remains.
That choice is not right. The full first-8-hour total is the number you just worked out, but some of it is already in.
Ask how much is still owed before you set the rate.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the subtraction. Fluid given before arrival belongs to the same total.

say.text: That choice is not right. The deduction is made, but the eight hours start at the wrong moment.
Reread the stem for when the clock started.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the clock. Think about when the first 8 hours began.

say.text: Start from the first-8-hour total, then ask how much of it the patient has already had and how many of the 8 hours are left.
Half of 4 x 50 x 40 is 4,000 mL due in the first 8 hours from the burn. Deduct the 1,000 mL given.
That leaves 3,000 mL over the six hours left, about 500 mL/h.
A patient arrives with an ambulance drip still running. Burn time and TBSA are confirmed.
What is the next step in the fluid plan?

choices.label: Start the full formula rate on top of the running drip
Work out the first-8-hour volume and subtract what has run in
Stop the drip and restart the formula from zero
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Fluid given before arrival is deducted from the first-8-hour volume, and the rate is then titrated hourly.
That choice is not right. Starting the formula as if nothing had been given adds a second dose to the first.
Ask what the patient has already received.

sure_note.text: You were sure the formula rate goes on top. Check what the running drip has already delivered.

say.text: That choice is not right. Restarting wipes out fluid the patient has already had, so the sum starts from the wrong place.
Ask whether earlier fluid still counts.

sure_note.text: You were sure the plan restarts. Check whether earlier fluid counts toward the total.

say.text: Before any rate is set, ask what the patient has already had and what the formula says is owed.
Work out the first-8-hour volume from the burn time, then deduct what the ambulance has given.
Run the remainder and titrate hourly to urine output.
Two adults, both with 40% burns, start on the same rate. Patient A passes 12 mL/h of urine. Patient B passes 90 mL/h.
What does each need?

choices.label: Raise B's rate and lower A's
Leave both at the starting rate
Raise A's rate and lower B's
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Low urine means more fluid; high urine means less.
The same starting rate was split by what each patient's urine showed.
That choice is not right. When the numbers look ordinary, holding the starting rate is the easy default, but these two patients differ.
Ask whether opposite urine readings can need the same rate.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the starting rate. It is an estimate to be adjusted from urine output.

say.text: That choice is not right. More urine can look like more fluid going in, so high output seems to need more, but that reads the gauge backwards.
Read each number as a sign of whether the tissues are full or short.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction for each patient. Think about what each reading says about perfusion.

say.text: Read each patient's urine against the target. Which one shows tissues that are short of fluid?
Patient A's low output means under-perfusion, so A's rate rises.
Patient B's high output means B's rate comes down, to avoid overload.
A 2-year-old arrives with a scald over the head and both legs.
How do you estimate the burn's TBSA?

choices.label: Lund and Browder chart, which adjusts for age
Wallace rule of nines, as for an adult
Rule of nines, with the legs counted double
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Head and legs are what differ most, so an age-adjusted chart is the right tool for this child.
That choice is not right. The rule of nines is the method you know best, but its shares are set for adults.
Ask what the stem tells you about the patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the adult rule. Check the patient's age before choosing a chart.

say.text: That choice is not right. Changing one figure shows you noticed legs differ, but it still uses the adult scheme and the adult leg share.
Ask which way each leg's share moves in a child.

sure_note.text: You were sure of a doubled-leg adjustment. Check the leg and head shares for a young child.

say.text: Burns on the head and both legs are where a child's body differs most from an adult's. Which method accounts for age?
Use a Lund and Browder chart. A young child's head is about 18% and each leg about 14%.
The adult rule of nines overestimates the legs and underestimates the head in children.
A man's forearm is burned all the way round.
Which description needs an escharotomy now?

choices.label: Deep partial-thickness, all the way round, with blisters
Full-thickness, all the way round, with the fingers going pale
Superficial red burn over the whole chest, breathing normally
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The full-thickness ring is what compromises the limb, and pale fingers signal it.
Release the eschar now.
That choice is not right. A deep burn that blisters looks severe, but depth is only one of the qualifiers.
Check the depth qualifier first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the depth qualifier. Think about which depth forms a rigid eschar.

say.text: That choice is not right. A burn over a whole chest feels like a crisis, but size does not decide this.
Check the depth and whether breathing is restricted.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check both qualifiers: depth and whether breathing is restricted.

say.text: Escharotomy releases a tight, unyielding crust. What must the crust be like, and what must it be doing to the limb?
Escharotomy is for circumferential full-thickness limb burns with distal ischaemia or falling pulses, and for chest burns that restrict breathing.
Incisions go through eschar only, along the midlateral and midaxial lines.
Why does a full-thickness ring of burn threaten the limb?

choices.label: Any deep burn forms eschar, so release it at once
Heat destroys the main artery, so the limb dies at once
Inelastic eschar constricts as swelling builds, squeezing vessels
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The eschar cannot stretch, so swelling compresses the vessels. That is why the cut releases the pressure.
That choice is not right. Depth feels like the cause, because deep burns look the most dangerous.
Ask what squeezes the limb as swelling builds.

sure_note.text: You were sure depth was the cause. Think about what happens to a ring that cannot stretch.

say.text: That choice is not right. Heat injury to the skin does not by itself cut off the main artery.
Ask what changes over the hours after the burn and what it presses on.
Picture a tight, unyielding ring around a limb that is swelling inside it.
A full-thickness eschar does not stretch. As oedema builds under it, the eschar constricts the vessels and the distal limb is starved.

cards.q: Urine output is low on a burn drip. What do you do to the rate?
cards.a: Raise it by about 20-25% and recheck hourly; the formula is only a starting estimate.

cards.q: Urine output targets: adult, child, electrical injury with myoglobinuria?
cards.a: Adult 0.5 mL/kg/h (30-50 mL/h); child 1 mL/kg/h; electrical about 1-1.5 mL/kg/h (75-100 mL/h in an adult).

cards.q: Ambulance has already given fluid. How is the first-8-hour volume handled?
cards.a: Deduct it from the first-8-hour volume, counted from the time of burn, and run the remainder.

cards.q: Which method estimates TBSA in a young child, and why?
cards.a: Lund and Browder chart: head about 18%, each leg about 14%, so the adult rule of nines misleads.
Circumferential full-thickness limb burns with distal ischaemia, and chest burns restricting ventilation; inelastic eschar constricts as oedema builds.
